content: At the end of 2014, a total of 26 substances, including 16 pesticides, were listed in the annexes of the relevant convention. The most current list of these substances can be accessed on the convention's official website. Many of these chemicals are also included under the Rotterdam Convention. Article 3 of the convention specifies strict prohibitions on chemicals listed in Annex A, requiring contracting parties to eliminate their production, use, import, and export. It also outlines restrictions on the production and use of chemicals listed in Annex B. However, imports of these chemicals for environmentally sound disposal are exempted. Specific exemptions for production and use are also provided for certain chemicals in Annexes A and B, such as those used for disease vector control under Part II of the annex. Consequently, parties to the convention are obligated to prohibit the production and use of most listed chemicals at the national level. The convention also establishes requirements for the management of persistent organic pollutant (POP) stockpiles and wastes. The Basel Convention, which came into force in 1992, regulates the international shipment of hazardous wastes. While not specifically targeting pesticides, it addresses obsolete pesticides and substances that may be by-products or waste products from pesticides. This convention is particularly useful for national governments aiming to prevent the dumping of waste products, such as obsolete pesticides, within their borders, especially in cases where governments lack the capacity to manage these wastes in an environmentally sound manner. The Basel Convention defines hazardous wastes as those falling under categories listed in Annex I and exhibiting characteristics outlined in Annex III. Annex I includes wastes from the production, formulation, and use of biocides (pesticides), while Annex III covers substances or wastes that can cause death, serious injury, or harm to human health if ingested, inhaled, or absorbed through the skin. It also includes substances or wastes that may have delayed or chronic effects, such as carcinogenicity. Under the Basel Convention, parties may prohibit the import of hazardous wastes or specific types of hazardous waste shipments. Exporting states are required to provide prior written notification to the importing state and obtain written consent before moving hazardous wastes across borders. Although the convention primarily focuses on transboundary waste movement, it also imposes obligations on parties to develop national legislation, ensure adequate disposal facilities, establish criminal penalties for violations, and require proper labeling, packaging, and documentation for hazardous waste shipments. The Montreal Protocol addresses substances that deplete the ozone layer, including one specific pesticide, methyl bromide. Industrialized countries were required to eliminate the production of methyl bromide by January 2005, with certain exceptions for pre-shipment, quarantine, emergency uses, and critical-use exemptions. These exemptions are temporary and strictly limited, intended for cases where technically and economically feasible alternatives are not immediately available. Some developing countries have agreed to phase out methyl bromide on an accelerated timeline. Several International Labour Organization (ILO) conventions address the safety and health of workers exposed to chemicals, particularly in agriculture. The C184 Safety and Health in Agriculture Convention, adopted in 2001 and effective in 2003, aims to close gaps in national legislation that often fail to protect agricultural workers through occupational health and safety laws. Many individuals exposed to pesticides during their work are not covered, especially informal laborers. The ILO Convention No. 182 on the Worst Forms of Child Labour, adopted in 1999, has a high ratification rate and calls for the elimination of work harmful to children's health, safety, or morals, including pesticide application due to children's increased vulnerability to toxic effects. The Agriculture Convention imposes responsibilities on employers, strengthens workers' rights, and requires governments to develop coherent national policies on agricultural safety and health, consult stakeholders, establish responsible authorities, and ensure inspection systems. The Chemical Weapons Convention (CWC) seeks to eliminate chemical weapons by prohibiting their development, production, acquisition, stockpiling, retention, transfer, or use. States Parties must destroy existing stockpiles and production facilities and establish verification regimes for certain toxic chemicals and their precursors to ensure they are used only for non-prohibited purposes. Non-binding international instruments, such as plans of action, declarations, codes of conduct, guidelines, and technical standards, promote international harmonization. The International Code of Conduct on Pesticide Management, adopted in 1985 and revised in 2002 and 2013, provides a reference framework for governments, the pesticide industry, and stakeholders. It is supported by technical guidelines offering detailed guidance on pesticide lifecycle management. Although voluntary, the Code has been widely adopted and influences national pesticide legislation. It encourages integrated pest management and outlines regulatory and technical requirements for effective pesticide management. The Codex Alimentarius Commission (CAC), a joint body of FAO and WHO, develops harmonized food standards, including maximum residue limits (MRLs) for pesticides. These MRLs are established by the Codex Committee on Pesticide Residues (CCPR) and are recognized by the World Trade Organization (WTO). Some governments adopt Codex MRLs as legally binding standards to align national regulations with international consensus. The Globally Harmonized System of Classification and Labelling of Chemicals (GHS) is an internationally agreed tool for chemical hazard communication, covering all chemicals, including pesticides. Developed as part of Agenda 21 in 1992, GHS ensures that information on chemical hazards is available in a harmonized format on labels and safety data sheets worldwide. GHS classification includes chronic human toxicity and environmental toxicity, making it more comprehensive than the WHO Classification of Pesticides by Hazard. An increasing number of countries are adopting GHS as a binding standard through national legislation. Countries can meet their international legal obligations through various approaches, such as explicitly incorporating treaty obligations into national law, transposing treaty requirements into national legislation, or adjusting national laws to align with international instruments while considering local policies and resources. The latter approach is often the most effective, as international provisions are typically general, allowing countries to determine implementation strategies suited to their contexts.
